## Critics of the multiverse {#the-multiverse-has-its-critics .smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. Our curve keeps the **`r format(nrow(spec_curve), big.mark = ",")`** specifications that a review of every option judged justifiable for this claim, and a decomposition by fork does the job that every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen
- "**There is only one correct analysis**" once the question is fully specified [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne] – your preregistered specification guards against *cherry-picking*, and their deeper point is that preregistering a choice does not yet make it *justified*, which is what the estimand and DAG work were for
- "What's a multiverse **good for** anyway?" – reflection, persuasion, or inference, and each purpose needs a *differently built* universe [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood]. Our full menu serves **reflection** and the curated curve moves towards **persuasion**; how much more to read into it is the open debate
:::

::: {.src}
The book-length how-to: @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational; the estimand diagnosis of the red-card study: @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
The method that you practised is the subject of a live debate, which you can now read for yourself. Katrin Auspurg, who with Josef Brüderl traced the spread in the red-card study to teams answering different questions, answered a study of three point six billion estimates with the line at the top of the slide, that only thoughtful, justified models belong in a curve. Our curve is built as she recommends, since every option of the menu was reviewed for whether it is a justifiable answer to this claim, and the decomposition by fork does the one job that every critic endorses, which is to locate where the argument has to take place. Lakens and colleagues argue that once the question is fixed, only one analysis implements it correctly. A preregistered specification guards against cherry-picking, and their deeper point, that preregistering a choice does not make it justified, is why the graph comes before the preregistration. Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask what a multiverse is for. Our full menu serves reflection, and the curated curve, with a published reason for every option, moves towards persuasion; how much more can be read into it is the open question of the debate that you have now joined.
:::

## Identifying the one correct analysis {#how-would-you-know .smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
On the red cards, twenty-nine teams modelled one count as **linear, logistic or Poisson**: claims about how the outcome was generated that cannot all be right, so on the argument of Lakens and colleagues most of that spread is error.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Grant the argument, and suppose that **one correct analysis exists**. Which one is it?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Getting there needs the estimand *and* the identification assumptions *and* agreement about the measurement – and on this claim, reasonable people disagree about all three.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So the curve complements the one-correct-analysis view: it is a **map of the disagreement that remains**, drawn because we cannot yet settle it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And it points at what to argue about: on this claim, at the **estimator** – whether the comparison removes what all member states shared in a year – and at the **predictor**.
:::
::::

@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne

Lakens and colleagues argue that a research question, once fully specified, implies one analysis that estimates its quantity, so that a spread of results indicates that most specifications are wrong rather than that diversity is legitimate. [advance] In the red-card study the twenty-nine teams modelled one count as linear, logistic or Poisson, claims about how the outcome was generated that cannot all be right, so on this reading most of the spread is error, and I think that the argument is largely right. [advance] Granting the argument, suppose that one correct analysis exists; the next question is which one it is, and how we would know. [advance] I therefore read the curve as a companion to the view that there is one correct analysis rather than as its rival, a map of the disagreement that remains, drawn because we cannot yet settle it. ## What preregistration settles {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does settle**

- That your specification was not chosen *because of* the result
- That your rule for what counts as support was fixed before you had a result
- That a reader can see what you intended, and what you changed
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does not settle**

- Whether the specification was **any good**
- Whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies
- Whether the assumptions behind it hold

A badly reasoned analysis that is preregistered is still badly reasoned; the preregistration only adds a timestamp
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
That is why the estimand and the DAG came **first** today: preregistration protects a choice, and the causal reasoning is what justifies it.
:::

::: notes
Preregistration settles a limited set of things, and the two columns weigh equally. It settles that your specification was not chosen because of the result that it gave, that your rule for what counts as support was fixed before you had a result to bend it around, and that a reader can tell what you intended and what you changed afterwards, guarantees that no other device provides. It does not settle whether the specification was any good, whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies, or whether its assumptions hold, and a badly reasoned analysis that is preregistered remains badly reasoned, with a timestamp on it. [advance] That is why we wrote the estimand and drew the graph first, since preregistration protects a choice and the causal reasoning justifies it.
:::
